chunks.content: 1 Introduction Post‐stroke epilepsy (PSE) contributes to a substantial proportion of epilepsy burden, especially in older adults, where it accounts for half of all the new epilepsy cases [ ]. Our population is rapidly aging. Substantial effort has, therefore, been made in the last decade to create prognostic PSE models. The two most used predictive models for individualized PSE prognostication are the CAVE score for intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) and the SeLECT score for ischemic stroke [ , ]. The SeLECT score includes five predictors: severity of stroke (NIHSS), large‐artery atherosclerosis etiology, early seizure (</ = 7 days), cortical involvement, and territory of the middle cerebral artery (MCA) [ ]. It was developed and validated in a European cohort. While several iterations of the SeLECT score have been published, we lack large‐scale studies to validate and improve the SeLECT score in geographically diverse populations, especially in the United States [ ]. A major barrier to applying the SeLECT score in large datasets is the need to manually extract MCA and cortical involvement from neuroimaging or clinical notes. These features are not routinely or consistently coded and require expert review of imaging or detailed electronic health records (EHRs) chart review. Recent neuroimaging research on lesion mapping found that the volume of post‐stroke chronic encephalomalacia is strongly associated with epilepsy development [ ]. Acute neuroimaging data for the CAVE score found ICH volume to be a significant predictor of epilepsy development when it is more than 10 mL [ ]. However, the SeLECT model did not consider the role of volume of acute ischemic stroke in PSE and only included two binary neuroimaging predictors (cortical and MCA territory involvement) [ , ]. Advances in machine learning and artificial intelligence have allowed automated tools for calculating ischemic stroke volumes using diffusion‐weighted imaging (DWI) [ , ]. The goal of our study was to determine if the size of acute ischemic stroke is a significant predictor of PSE and if its use can help overcome the limitation of manual extraction of neuroimaging data used in the SeLECT score. 2 Methods After institutional review board approval, we conducted a retrospective, single‐center study at the Cleveland Clinic in Cleveland, OH, USA. The study included adults with acute stroke admissions from January 2013 to October 2018, and DWI data from acute Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI). Cortical and MCA territory involvement was independently extracted by two board‐certified neurologists (VD and VP). Disagreements were mutually resolved. We obtained data on each variable of the SeLECT score through manual extraction from the EHRs. Patients without an MRI during admission or insufficient data to calculate the SeLECT score were excluded. Using these variables, we computed the SeLECT score for each patient in our sample. Clinical seizures during hospital admission and follow‐up, determined and documented in the EHR by a licensed healthcare provider, were extracted. A clinical seizure within ≤7 days of stroke was classified as an acute symptomatic seizure (ASyS), and a seizure > 7 days after stroke was classified as a PSE [ ]. 2.1 MRI Acquisition Clinically acquired MRIs were obtained retrospectively through the Picture Archiving and Communication System. Axial diffusion‐weighted echo planar images, including b = 0 and trace (b‐value = 1000 s/mm 2 ), were used to calculate the ischemic stroke volume. The sequence median (interquartile range [IQR]) parameters were echo time = 114 (98, 114) ms, repetition time = 3802 (3500, 4200) ms, in‐plane pixel resolution = 1.8 (1.7, 1.8) mm, and slice thickness = 7.0 (7.0, 7.0) mm. 2.2 DWI Analysis The training datasets came from a separate cohort of 175 patients with their first acute ischemic stroke, incomplete outcomes, or missing baseline MRI [ ]. The b0 and trace images were used to segment regions of hyperintense areas on trace images. For the training and validation, we manually segmented hyperintense DWI regions with consultation with a neuroradiologist (Appendix Figure ). The median DWI volume (IQR) was 3.0 (0.8−10.3) mL. We developed a convolutional neural network with a 2D U‐Net architecture [ ]. Briefly, the architecture had six levels with skip connections, and each unit with convolutions and batch normalization layers. The data were split into training, validation, and testing sets as a 5:1:1 ratio. The mean Dice coefficient on the validation dataset was 0.87, and the testing dataset was 0.81, which was within a typical range [ ]. The Dice similarity coefficient score is a statistical measure used to quantify the spatial overlap between two binary segmentations, typically, the automated segmentation output and the ground truth manual segmentation, of stroke lesions in neuroimaging studies [ ]. The Dice similarity coefficient score is a statistical measure used to quantify the spatial overlap between two binary segmentations, typically, the automated segmentation output and the ground truth manual segmentation, of stroke lesions in neuroimaging studies [ ]. As a post‐processing, we used the b0 and trace images to calculate the maps of apparent diffusion coefficients (ADCs), and the hypointense ADC areas were retained if the lesion‐wise 25th percentile ADC value was smaller than 600×10 −6 mm 2 /s and if the lesion size is 4 voxels or greater with an 18‐connectivity. The results were visually checked by a rater and modified if necessary. For external validation, we applied the model to the Ischemic Stroke Lesion Segmentation 2022 (ISLES22) training dataset, consisting of 250 studies [ ]. Briefly, ISLES22 included subjects 18 years or older who had received MR imaging of the brain for previously diagnosed or suspected stroke. The MRI protocols included FLAIR and DWI trace images at a b‐value of up to 1000 s/mm 2 , as well as an ADC map at a 2 mm isotropic resolution. The zero‐shot validation showed a median Dice (IQR) of 0.65 (0.38, 0.76). However, the median (IQR) DWI lesion volume in ISLES 22 was 6.66 (1.58, 21.2) mL, which was larger than the internal training dataset ( t ‐test, p <0.001). After the model was fine‐tuned to ISLES22, the Dice improved to 0.82 (0.65, 0.88). 2.3 Statistical Analysis Descriptive statistics were computed for the entire cohort and stratified by whether the patient developed PSE. Mean with standard deviation or median with IQR was used for continuous variables, and frequency with percentage was used for categorical variables. Comparisons were made using two‐sample t ‐tests or Wilcoxon rank sum tests for continuous variables and Fisher's exact test for categorical variables. We first applied the published point‐based SeLECT score to our cohort [ ]. Then, we refit the SeLECT model in our cohort by re‐estimating the coefficients of its original predictors using a multivariable Cox proportional hazards model with time to PSE as the outcome. This allowed us to assess how the published SeLECT model performed in our data and to compare it with both the refit model and the additional models we developed. Patients who did not develop PSE were censored at their last follow‐up date. The proportional hazards assumption was evaluated using Schoenfeld residuals, and no major violations were detected. We then fit various models by adding stroke volume and then removing one or both of cortical involvement and MCA. Stroke volume was modeled as a continuous variable (per 10 mL). Nonlinearity was examined visually, and no major deviations from linearity were observed. Therefore, the total number of models that were fit includes the following: Refit SeLECT model (NIHSS + LAA + early seizure + cortical involvement + MCA) SeLECT + stroke volume SeLECT + stroke volume—cortical involvement SeLECT + stroke volume—MCA SeLECT + stroke volume—cortical involvement—MCA For each of these models, we compared discrimination using the concordance index (C‐index). Model calibration was examined graphically. We internally validated each of these models using bootstrapping with 500 iterations. To determine whether the optimism‐corrected C‐index was different between models, we used bootstrapping with 1000 bootstrap samples to compute 95% confidence intervals for the difference between each pair of optimism‐corrected C‐index values. Furthermore, for clinical use purposes, we analyzed whether there was a stroke volume threshold beyond which the size of the stroke is significantly more predictive of PSE. Because time to PSE is a time‐dependent outcome, we performed time‐dependent receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, where time to PSE was the dependent variable, and stroke volume was the predictor. Specifically, we used the cumulative sensitivity and dynamic specificity method [ ]. We created ROC curves for each of the 6‐month, 1‐year, and 2‐year periods, and the area under the ROC curve (AUC), along with a 95% confidence interval, was computed. The optimal cutoff point for stroke volume was determined at each time point using Youden's index (the maximum vertical distance from the ROC curve to the diagonal line) [ ]. The sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) at each time point, based on the corresponding stroke volume cutoff, were estimated. All computations were performed in R, version 4.3.1 [ ]. All tests were two‐sided, and statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. 3 Results Of the 375 patients qualifying for the study criteria, 221 had both DWI data and data for all SeLECT variables and were included in the final analysis. Compared with the study cohort ( N = 221), excluded patients had significantly more frequent cortical involvement and higher NIHSS scores, resulting in higher SeLECT

Compared with the study cohort ( N = 221), excluded patients had significantly more frequent cortical involvement and higher NIHSS scores, resulting in higher SeLECT scores (Appendix Table ). Representative examples of automated DWI lesion segmentation are shown in Figure . Cortical involvement on initial Computed Tomography (CT) is strongly associated with higher NIHSS [ , ]. The confirmation of stroke on the initial CT scan explains the lower likelihood of undergoing a subsequent MRI, leading to their exclusion from the current analysis. The mean age of the study cohort was 63.5 (±13.8) years and included 51% females. MRIs were acquired on Siemens systems in 96% of patients, with 93% from 1.5T scanners and the remainder from 3T scanners. During a median follow‐up of 59 months (IQR, 25–79), 35 (15.8%) patients developed PSE. Table shows descriptive statistics for the study cohort, stratified by their PSE status. On unadjusted analyses (Table ), patients who developed PSE had significantly higher SeLECT score, were more likely to have ASyS, and had larger stroke volume. Table shows the results of the models we examined. The original SeLECT score had a C‐index of 0.669 in our sample. Our refit SeLECT model had an optimism‐corrected C‐index of 0.642. Stoke volume remained an independently significant predictor of PSE in all models. Adding stroke volume to the SeLECT model resulted in an optimism‐corrected C‐index of 0.656. Keeping stroke volume while removing only cortical involvement or MCA territory resulted in an optimism‐corrected C‐index of 0.664 and 0.668, respectively. Keeping stroke volume but removing both cortical involvement and MCA resulted in an optimism‐corrected C‐index of 0.679. Table presents the differences in optimism‐corrected C‐index values for each pair of models, along with 95% confidence intervals. Given that all 95% confidence interval differences contained the null value of 0, we conclude that none of the models had significantly higher or lower optimism‐corrected C‐index values. Calibration was generally good for all models, as shown in Figure . Given that stroke volume is a statistically significant predictor in all models, we post hoc evaluated a threshold at which it becomes more predictive of PSE. Figure shows ROC curves for stroke volume at 6‐month, 1‐year, and 2‐year post‐stroke. Table shows the AUC, optimal stroke volume cutoff point, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, and NPV for each time point. AUC was higher for earlier time points. Stroke volume cutoff points varied by time point and ranged from 11.6 to 16.7 mL. 4 Discussion We found that acute stroke volume is a significant and independent predictor of PSE. There was a 12% increased risk of PSE for every 10 mL increase in stroke volume, which remained a significant predictor across all models. The predictive performance (discrimination and calibration) of the SeLECT model, when the stroke volume substitutes for both cortical and MCA involvement, was comparable to that of the original SeLECT score. This lack of significant difference in model performance, and stroke volume remaining a strong predictor across various models, suggests that it can reliably serve as a practical, automated proxy for the current neuroimaging components of the SeLECT score. Automated DWI‐based lesion segmentation has now become feasible and accurate, achieving a Dice coefficient in the range of 0.81−0.85 [ , ]. These methods are robust to variations in scanner type and image quality. They have been validated in multicenter cohorts [ , ]. Our DWI‐based volume analysis algorithm achieved a Dice coefficient on our internal dataset (0.87) and the external dataset (0.82), comparable to those of the Artifical Intelligence (AI) tools in the literature. Additionally, segmentation error is unlikely to bias our results meaningfully, as measurement error in stroke volume would tend to attenuate effect estimates rather than create spurious associations. Given the strong and consistent association across all models, the predictive value of stroke volume appears robust. The availability of open‐source, state‐of‐the‐art, and reliable tools for ischemic stroke volume calculation enables the calculation to be performed at scale for large datasets [ ]. In addition, researchers have developed validated, automated methods to extract NIHSS scores from EHRs using natural language processing [ ]. In addition, researchers have developed validated, automated methods to extract NIHSS scores from EHRs using natural language processing [ ]. With both NIHSS and stroke volume now extractable at scale, most of the core predictors for PSE risk can be assembled without manual review, enabling efficient, reproducible, large‐scale research and clinical implementation. A very recent systematic review found that the SeLECT score's application in various geographical locations, including China, Turkey, and Japan, has limitations in its discrimination of PSE and is yet to be tested in an exclusively US population [ ]. Our study, to our knowledge, is the first application of the SeLECT score in a US cohort, demonstrating a more than 10% loss in its discriminatory power for predicting PSE (c‐index of 0.77 vs. 0.64) [ ]. This difference may reflect racial differences in PSE risk as shown in several extensive studies. The Northern Manhattan Study found that PSE risk was two ‐to three‐fold higher in Hispanics and non‐Hispanic Blacks compared to non‐Hispanic Whites [ ]. Similarly, the Cardiovascular Health Study and the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) study have found a higher risk of PSE among Black participants, with risk factors like hypertension and diabetes exerting a more substantial effect in these minority populations [ , ]. When placed in the context of chronic lesional studies, our finding suggests that the volume of brain injury plays a critical role in epileptogenesis from the acute to the chronic pathological stages of stroke [ ]. It is noteworthy that, like the CAVE score, it seems that the minimum ischemic stroke volume that significantly increases PSE is more than 10 mL [ ]. Limitations of this study include the retrospective, single‐center approach. Additionally, more severe stroke patients and those with cortical involvement on CT scan did not receive MRI and hence, were excluded from the current analysis. To overcome this selection bias and increase the generalizability of the stroke volume as a robust PSE predictor, we plan to evaluate it using automated tools that use CT scans [ ]. Additionally, future multicenter studies with larger sample sizes are needed to validate our findings and create new prognostic models that utilize stroke volume to predict PSE [ ]. Overall, stroke volume provides a more precise and quantitative measure of acute brain injury than binary regional designations. Our findings indicate that automated DWI‐based volume estimation can serve as a practical alternative to manually abstracted cortical and MCA involvement. Automated segmentation is feasible and sufficiently accurate, and it substantially reduces the burden of manual data extraction. Incorporating stroke volume into prognostic modeling may enhance the efficiency and objectivity of PSE risk prediction and, with further validation, could become a preferred imaging‐based predictor. chunks.content: Background The selective synaptic vesicle protein 2A (SV2A) ligand brivaracetam has been approved as a seizure suppressant drug in Europe since 2016. Compared to its predecessor drug levetiracetam (LEV), BRV binds to the SV2A protein with a 15- to 30-fold greater affinity without simultaneous modulation of the AMPA receptor [ ]. With a significant reduction in seizures with additional treatment with BRV, various studies have demonstrated good overall tolerability of the new antiseizure medication (ASM) as well as a reduced occurrence of psychiatric undesirable drug effects such as depression and irritability compared to LEV [ , , , ]. The risks of neurodevelopmental disorders and congenital malformations during pregnancy with antiseizure medication such as levetiracetam or lamotrigine are considered to be relatively low [ ]. Due to significant fluctuations in serum levels, dosage adjustments are often necessary during pregnancy with lamotrigine and levetiracetam [ ]. Although an increase in prescriptions of newer ASM such as BRV can be observed [ ], little is known about the teratogenic effects of BRV and potential serum level fluctuations during pregnancy. In a retrospective multicenter study, Steinig et al. [ ] examined post-marketing effects like efficacy, retention and tolerability in 262 patients with epilepsy who received brivaracetam as add-on therapy. During the observation period, two pregnancies occurred while taking BRV. As soon as the pregnancy became known, antiseizure medication was switched back to levetiracetam in accordance with the guidelines. Both pregnancies continued after temporary use of BRV. In 2020, a first case series of three women with epilepsy treated with brivaracetam during pregnancy was reported by Paolini and colleagues: The daily dose of BRV intake ranged from 50 mg/d to 200 mg/d. While two patients received BRV as monotherapy, the third received lamotrigine (LTG) as a comedication. Minor congenital malformations such as infantile hemangioma, congenital dermal melanocytosis and ankyloglossia were observed in two of three children (see Table ). Navarro et al. [ ] reported the birth of a healthy child on BRV therapy during pregnancy in a patient with therapy-refractory juvenile myoclonic epilepsy. Landmark and colleagues [ ] reported three healthy births during pregnancy with brivaracetam in two patients with epilepsy: Whereas one patient received BRV in monotherapy, the other also received perampanel and lacosamide as comedication. During pregnancy, serum levels of BRV remained stable in both patients. While the serum levels of BRV in the umbilical cord of both twins of one patient were reported as comparable to the blood concentration of their mother as measured one hour after last dose intake (infant/mother ratios: 1.1), BRV serum level in the umbilical cord of another newborn was reported as low (infant/mother ratio: 0.18) compared to its mother´s level as measured 9.5 h hours after last dose intake (see Table ). Case report Here we report a 31-year-old right-handed female patient who presented with pregnancy while being treated with BRV and TPM. She had focal, non-aware seizures occurring several times per week. During the seizures, she felt tachycardia and dizziness and did not respond to speech. In her past medical history, the patient reported febrile seizures that had occurred at the age of 6 years and a traumatic brain injury at the age of 11 years. The patient was medically refractory to lamotrigine (LTG) and levetiracetam (LEV). Due to the diagnosis of drug-resistant epilepsy, presurgical video-EEG monitoring was performed in 2014 and right occipital lobe epilepsy was diagnosed. A 3-Tesla cMRI showed no evidence of epileptogenic lesions. The patient refused any operative procedure. Subsequently, various antiseizure medications were given due to inadequate seizure control or side effects, such as zonisamide (ZNS), topiramate (TPM), valproate (VPA), carbamazepine (CBZ), oxcarbazepine (OXC), perampanel (PER), gabapentin (GBP) and BRV. In December 2021, the patient reported that she was pregnant, and was already 17 weeks pregnant. She presented with BRV (200 mg/d) and TPM (200 mg/d) and a seizure frequency of one per day. Serum levels of antiseizure medications, taken approximately 6 h after the morning doses, were 2.91 mg/l for BRV and 4.7 mg/l for TPM. The patient was already taking folic acid supplementation daily during pregnancy (5 mg/d). There was no switch back to levetiracetam, as is usual during pregnancy, as the patient refused this due to ineffectiveness and intolerance to this medication in the past. Due to the advanced pregnancy, it was assumed that organogenesis had already been completed. After detailed explanation, we decided together to continue the previous antiseizure medication. We agreed on monthly outpatient follow-ups. During those, the serum levels of antiseizure medication were stable (see Table ). Since the patient was only able to attend appointments in the early afternoon, drug levels were taken 6 h after the last dose. Seizure frequency during pregnancy was unchanged. At week 39, the patient gave spontaneous birth to a healthy daughter (Apgar score: 9/10/10). 1.5 h

The serum ratio of BRV (infant/mother) was 0.58 and serum ratio of TPM was 0.56. One month after delivery, the patient presented to our outpatient clinic. Her serum level of BRV was relatively stable (3.32 mg/l) comparable to the serum levels during pregnancy, whereas the serum level of TPM increased (7.3 mg/l). Seizure frequency was unchanged. Eight months after delivery, the patient returned to our outpatient clinic. She had stopped breastfeeding 6 months after delivery. The daughter was healthy and appropriately developed. BRV and TPM were still taken with unchanged daily dosage. Due to recent data on the increased risk of carcinoma with daily folic acid supplementation of more than 1 mg [ ], folic acid therapy was reduced to 0.8 mg daily. Discussion We report a 34-year-old patient with difficult-to-treat pharmacoresistant epilepsy who gave birth to a healthy child after pregnancy with topiramate and brivaracetam. Topiramate may be associated with an increased incidence of major congenital malformations: Based on data from 7355 pregnancies in the EURAP study group, Tomson and colleagues showed that 6 of 152 pregnancies (3.9%) with topiramate lead to major congenital malformation, such as cardiac malformation or hypospadias [ , ]. A review of the Cochrane database also showed that prenatal exposure to topiramate may lead to facial malformations [ ]. A systematic review by Schmidt and colleagues [ ] examining umbilical cord transmission of ASM found that antiseizure medication associated with an increased risk of congenital malformations, such as TPM, CBZ or VPA showed relevant differences among each other with respect to penetration into the fetal circulation. Regarding topiramate, the authors reported an intermediate penetration rate of topiramate into the umbilical cord with a comparatively high penetration of TPM into breast milk. Due to the risk of congenital malformations, fetal growth impairments and possible neuropsychiatric developmental disorders, the drug commission of the German medical association published a red hand letter in November 2023 with restrictions to prevent exposure to topiramate during pregnancy [ ]. Although an increasing use of newer ASM like SV2A ligand brivaracetam can be observed [ , ], evidence on newer antiseizure medication during pregnancy is scarce, particularly regarding therapeutic drug monitoring. The SV2A ligand brivaracetam is rapidly absorbed. According to previous evidence in healthy volunteers on BRV monotherapy, a dose-dependent peak in serum concentration is reached 2 h after ingestion with a plasma half-life of 9 h [ , , ]. To our knowledge the study by Landmark and colleagues [ ] is the first to provide pharmacokinetic data on brivaracetam in pregnancy and lactation. Landmark and colleagues determined serum concentrations 3 h after ingestion of 75 mg BRV (P1) and 9.5 h after ingestion of 100 mg BRV (P2). At P1 this was 0.81 mg/l. At P2 this was 1.4 mg/l. However, P2 was also on comedication with LCM and PER. The serum concentrations of BRV remained relatively stable in our patient, when 100 mg of BRV was taken twice daily. Since our patient was only able to attend appointments in the early afternoon, drug levels were taken at latest 6 h after the last dose intake. Compared to P1 in Landmark and colleagues, the concentration of BRV in our patient was higher despite a later blood sample. Compared to P2 in Landmark and colleagues, the concentration of BRV in the blood was also higher, with the same BRV dose but earlier blood sampling. Possible reasons for these results could be pharmacogenetic factors as well as metabolic influences of comedication with topiramate. Although there is little evidence regarding pregnancy and birth with newer ASM such as brivaracetam, the present case demonstrated that an uncomplicated pregnancy and healthy childbirth is possible. as metabolic influences of comedication with topiramate. Although there is little evidence regarding pregnancy and birth with newer ASM such as brivaracetam, the present case demonstrated that an uncomplicated pregnancy and healthy childbirth is possible. In a questionnaire-based survey, Mann and colleagues examined the knowledge of women with epilepsy (WWE) about their disease in a multicenter study between October and December 2020 and compared these results with data from 2005. Regarding disease-specific knowledge, there were no significant group differences in the cohort between 2005 and 2020. The authors found that special life events, like pregnancy in women with epilepsy, are associated with worries and false beliefs, which may lead to a reduction in ASM during pregnancy or a delayed medical consultation. The lack of knowledge correlated with lower educational level and with an elderly age. Due to the fact, that women with epilepsy are more likely to have unplanned pregnancies [ ], regular neurological-epileptological consultations should take place. In these, the change to ASM should be discussed regularly and in line with the patient`s prior knowledge if she wishes to have children. Furthermore, patients and their partners should be repeatedly informed, that a neurological consultation regarding a change or adjustment of the antiseizure medication should take place immediately after the pregnancy becomes known. Due to the fact, that half of epilepsies begin in childhood, the transition consultation should play a key role in providing information about epilepsy and pregnancy [ ]. In addition, interdisciplinary collaboration with gynecological colleagues should also be expanded. Finally, especially in the case of pregnancies under new antiseizure medications, reporting to pregnancy registries (e.g. EURAP) is necessary as well as an easier access to research databases [ ]. Conclusions Before or at latest when patients with ASM get pregnant, counselling should be performed by neurologist or epilepsy specialists to assess pharmacotherapy. Because there is little evidence regarding pregnancy with newer antiseizure medication, particularly regarding ASM concentrations, data donation to the pregnancy registries is important. Further data on the safety of brivaracetam during pregnancy are needed.

chunks.content: Introduction Status epilepticus (SE) represents a common neurological emergency associated with relevant morbidity and mortality. It can present at any age and in any location: the out-of-hospital setting, the emergency room, in-patients on any hospital ward, and patients already treated in the intensive care unit (ICU) for other reasons. If continuous intravenous anesthetic drugs are needed for its treatment, patients are typically transferred to the ICU. Definitions SE lacks a uniform biological marker and is a heterogeneous entity; it is defined as an epileptic seizure continuing beyond a certain time or recurring within the same timeframe before the patient recovers baseline clinical status [ ]. Ongoing seizures may be the consequence of mechanisms leading to prolonged paroxysmal neuronal discharges, or failure of pathways subtending seizure termination. illustrates temporal thresholds’ definition, the first corresponding to the typical duration of a given seizure type based on clinical observations, beyond which spontaneous termination of seizure activity is unlikely, while the second highlights the risk of subsequent neuronal damage; essentially relying on pre-clinical information [ ]. SE is classified using a syndromic approach, including clinical semiology ( ), etiology, electroencephalography (EEG) features, and age [ ]. An episode continuing clinically and/or on the electroencephalogram (EEG) despite administration of at least two antiseizure medications (ASM), typically including a benzodiazepine, is labeled refractory (RSE) [ ], and super-refractory (SRSE) if continuing despite at least one course of anesthetics [ ]. New-onset refractory SE (NORSE) occurs in previously healthy individuals lacking an obvious acute, structural or toxic-metabolic cause; a particular subgroup (febrile-induced refractory epilepsy syndrome, FIRES), originally described in children but now recognized to occur at any age, refers to its occurrence during a febrile illness preceding SE onset by 1–14 days [ ]. Epidemiology, etiologies, and diagnosis The annual SE incidence lies around 20–40/100,000, ranging possibly slightly higher in non-Caucasians [ , ]. The incidence is higher in the younger, and particularly in the elderly age groups, conferring a J-shaped curve [ ]. RSE accounts for roughly 1/3 rd , and SRSE for 1/20th of SE episodes [ ]. Up to half of patients suffering from SE have a previously known diagnosis of epilepsy [ , ]. In Europe, it has been calculated that an SRSE episode, by definition managed in the ICU, costs more than five times more than RSE, and ten times more than a readily treatment-responding episode that corresponds to roughly 4500 euros [ ], mirroring the situation in the United States [ ]. SE etiologies are very heterogeneous. In the industrialized world, acute or chronic cerebrovascular diseases, primary or metastatic brain tumors, brain trauma, toxic–metabolic disturbances, degenerative conditions, and anoxic–ischemic encephalopathy represent the underlying etiology of the majority of case [ , ], while in middle–low income countries [ ], childhood infections have a greater importance. Over the past decade, increasing attention has been directed toward autoimmune [including autoantibodies targeting cell-surface structures, such as N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors [ ]] and paraneoplastic etiologies, together accounting for a significant number of NORSE cases [ ]. While in adults, genetic (including mitochondrial) disorders are uncommon, these may be of much greater relevance in newborns and infants, together with inborn disorders of metabolism. Diagnosis of SE relies on the recognition of the clinical presentation, including timing, semiology, and biological situation of the patient, including age and previous comorbidities. EEG may be confirmatory for patients with convulsive SE, but is mandatory for detecting nonconvulsive SE. Up to 15% of ICU patients with impairment of consciousness of unclear cause may have nonconvulsive seizures [ , ] ( ), and a considerable proportion of patients with convulsive SE can show ongoing ictal activity on EEG after convulsion has stopped [ ]. On EEG, nonconvulsive SE should last longer than 10 min or be present for at least 20% of the recording. Importantly, it needs to fulfill the Salzburg EEG criteria, requiring either rhythmic or periodic discharges faster than 2.5 Hz, or the presence of additional criteria: spatial–temporal evolution, subtle clinical phenomena, or response to ASM [ ]. The interested reader is encouraged to refer to the updated American Clinical Neurophysiology Society terminology, providing generalizable classifications and labels to support communication between health care professionals [ ]. In the pre-hospital setting and in emergency rooms, the possibility of psychogenic non-epileptic events should be always kept in mind to prevent iatrogenic complications, particularly in patients with prolonged convulsions with forced eye closure, lacking oxygen desaturation and blood lactate elevation. In randomized trials on convulsive SE, up to 10% of patients presenting with prolonged convulsions had psychogenic events; 20% were admitted to the ICU [ ]; these patients may potentially develop iatrogenic complications. In randomized trials on convulsive SE, up to 10% of patients presenting with prolonged convulsions had psychogenic events; 20% were admitted to the ICU [ ]; these patients may potentially develop iatrogenic complications. In the ICU, conversely, it has been shown that while more than 90% of seizures/SE are nonconvulsive (thus only detectable with EEG), ¾ of patients showing abnormal movements actually do not seize [ ], highlighting the relevance of video-coupled EEG recordings. While continuous EEG (cEEG) is strongly recommended for patients receiving anesthetics for SE treatment (see below), the minimum duration of EEG in patients with suspected but not yet diagnosed seizures is somewhat debated. While recording up to 48 h is needed to detect 95% of seizures and SE in ICU patients [ ], clinical outcome does not seem to be markedly influenced by cEEG compared to repeated routine EEG. A recent trial showed that, despite significant higher sensitivity in terms of detection of ictal events, rhythmic or periodic EEG patterns, and more frequent treatment changes continuous EEG was not associated with improved survival at 6 months compared to repeated routine EEG [ ]. This is probably at least partly explained by the role of the underlying biological background (including etiology) that represents the main prognostic determinant; concomitant epileptiform activity, even if treated, is not always a modifiable prognostic factor [ ]. Depending on local resource availability, it is reasonable to apply the 2HELPS2B (frequency > 2 Hz; epileptiform discharges; lateralized or bilateral independent periodic discharges or lateralized rhythmic delta activity; “plus” features; any history of seizures; and brief potentially ictal rhythmic discharges) score to stratify the risk of subsequent seizure occurrence [ ]; it considers the prior occurrence of clinical seizures as well as the presence and frequency of rhythmic or periodic discharges, and of brief potentially ictal rhythmic discharges on initial EEG. The optimal EEG duration may be assessed with the TERSE (time-dependent electroclinical risk stratification for SE) algorithm [ ], encompassing type of consciousness impairment, occurrence of previous seizures, and of EEG epileptiform abnormalities, and/or rhythmic or periodic patterns. Treatment Initial measures The therapeutic approach to SE patients should be multimodal (diagnostic procedures parallel the administration of medications) and multidisciplinary, involving prehospital and emergency room caregivers, as well as neurologists, neuro-pediatricians, neurosurgeons, clinical neurophysiologists, and neuro-intensivists. Convulsive episodes tend to be recognized much faster than nonconvulsive ones [ ]; higher chances of control for convulsive episodes might possibly be in part related to earlier treatment initiation [ ]. Along the same line, liberal emergent use of EEG to quickly identify nonconvulsive SE in patients with unclear alteration of consciousness could in theory increase response to treatment. As in every medical emergency, prompt stabilization of airway and cardiovascular function is paramount. A comprehensive laboratory work-up accompanied in most cases by brain imaging should be performed quickly to identify the likely underlying etiology. As a rule of thumb, treatment directed toward the underlying cause, if identified, will have the highest change of success. Pharmacological treatments of SE are traditionally stratified into three consecutive steps of mostly intravenously administered compounds ( ). Adherence to published guidelines [ - ], mostly based on evidence from generalized convulsive SE, aims at minimizing the risk of incorrectly managed SE and may prevent evolution to RSE [ ]. First step: early status epilepticus Based on several randomized controlled trials [ , , ], benzodiazepines are the agents of choice: midazolam (which can also be administered intramuscularly), lorazepam, or clonazepam are all reasonable options, if dosed correctly [ ]. Although diazepam is sometimes used (intravenously, intrarectally, or intranasally) [ ], we do not recommend it if the previous alternatives are available. It has a quick onset of action due to its fast penetration in the central nervous system (CNS), but then undergoes a fast redistribution out of the CNS to peripheral fat tissue and is, thus, associated with a risk of early SE recurrence. Importantly, the risk of respiratory depression is higher with untreated ongoing seizure activity, compared to patients receiving benzodiazepines [ , ]. Adding a second agent to benzodiazepine in the pre-hospital setting did not improve seizure control or outcomes [ ]. Second step: established status epilepticus This includes non-sedating ASM often administered together with benzodiazepines; a recent trial demonstrated the equivalence of (fos-)phenytoin, valproate, and levetiracetam [ ]. Of note, valproate and phenytoin have complicated pharmacokinetic interactions, and a routine combination of them is not recommended. Alternatives include lacosamide [ ] or brivaracetam [ ], although they have been less well studied ( ). Third step: refractory status epilepticus Up to

ongoing seizure activity, compared to patients receiving benzodiazepines [ , ]. Adding a second agent to benzodiazepine in the pre-hospital setting did not improve seizure control or outcomes [ ]. Second step: established status epilepticus This includes non-sedating ASM often administered together with benzodiazepines; a recent trial demonstrated the equivalence of (fos-)phenytoin, valproate, and levetiracetam [ ]. Of note, valproate and phenytoin have complicated pharmacokinetic interactions, and a routine combination of them is not recommended. Alternatives include lacosamide [ ] or brivaracetam [ ], although they have been less well studied ( ). Third step: refractory status epilepticus Up to 30% of all SE episodes persist or recur despite first- and second-line treatments, a condition known as refractory SE (RSE); refractoriness is more likely in patients with acute symptomatic SE than a remote etiology or chronic epilepsy, in comatose patients, and when early SE treatment deviates from guidelines [ , ]. Guidelines for refractory generalized convulsive SE recommend ICU admission for anesthetic treatment [ , ]. A similar strategy is likely adequate for patients with NCSE in coma, including post-convulsive “subtle” SE, as these patients are typically already sedated and intubated. Conversely, patients with focal SE without marked impairment of consciousness might be safely managed outside the ICU with non-sedating IV ASM rather than anesthetics [ ]. Other add-on options in focal RSE (and SRSE) refractory include enterally administered ASM, such as pregabalin, topiramate or perampanel ( ). Achieving reliable steady-state concentrations in a short time frame with these agents requires high loading doses and can be challenging if enteral absorption is compromised (e.g., ileus or circulating shock). There is an ongoing controversy regarding the risk–benefit ratio of using anesthetics for SE. Several observational studies found an association between them and increased risk of complications and mortality [ - ]. While these attempted to adjust for some of the many possible confounders, such as age, SE semiology, and etiology, several other confounders were not always accounted for: taking into account SE refractoriness rendered the association between anesthetics and mortality no longer significant [ , ]. In fact, the previous findings are at odds with retrospective observations that high-dosed anesthetics [up to 3 mg/kg/h for midazolam, for example, [ , ]] and early coma induction [ , ] being associated with better SE control and lower mortality, although these studies did not formally compare anesthetics as second-line versus ASM as second-line treatment. Altogether, these studies suggest that the risk–benefit balance of anesthetic treatment is favorable in refractory convulsive and “subtle” post-convulsive SE ( ). The choice of drug, dosing, timing, and duration of exposure are as important as the decision to resort to coma induction. summarizes the reported anesthetics in SE. A recent multi-center retrospective study found that midazolam and propofol have comparable efficacy and safety [ ]; both appear as efficacious as barbiturates, while being associated with fewer complications, and shorter ICU stay or duration of mechanical ventilation [ , ]. Required doses might be relatively high ( and ) and need to be adjusted to reach EEG seizure control, rather than pre-specified target doses. As there is no evidence of superiority of one over the other, both propofol and midazolam may be used. Propofol has a shorter half-life, a theoretical advantage as rapid weaning should be avoided in patients with SE, but there is a risk of propofol infusion syndrome with prolonged infusions at > 5 mg/kg/h for > 24 h; hence, midazolam or a combination of lower doses of propofol with midazolam is preferred. The goal of treatment in RSE is seizure freedom. This is initially achieved by sequential administration of boluses of anesthetic drugs until seizures stop, together with the initiation of a maintenance infusion. Additional boluses and increases in infusion rate are often necessary to maintain seizure control. As almost half of patients treated for RSE will have mostly nonconvulsive seizures during treatment (“breakthrough seizures”; ), or at or after weaning off (“withdrawal seizures”) [ , ], aiming only for suppression of clinical seizures is not sufficient and video-EEG monitoring is necessary to allow control of nonconvulsive seizures, as well [ , , ]. Despite a paucity of supporting evidence, many experts will tolerate a few daily seizures to mitigate the risk of complications associated with profound sedation. Some evidence suggests that systematically aiming for EEG burst suppression ( ) or complete suppression is not necessary. Deeper levels of sedation are difficult to maintain with midazolam and are not associated with better SE control [ , ]. Association of deeper sedation with complications and worse outcomes has been shown [ , , ], although distinctions between direct toxic effects and the intrinsic severity of the underlying background are challenging to infer. The aim of “seizure suppression”, thus, represents a reasonable EEG target, accepting that some patients will require such high anesthetic doses that EEG background may be suppressed. There is a lack of evidence regarding the time during which anesthetics should be maintained once seizure freedom is achieved. Guidelines based on experts’ opinion suggest 24–48 h of sedation, but anecdotal evidence suggests that shorter therapy, at higher infusion rates, might be as effective and safer [ ]. Continuous EEG may help predict seizure recurrence upon weaning and tailor coma duration for each patient. High-amplitude [ ] or highly epileptiform bursts [ ] are associated with a higher risk of seizure recurrence and might motivate to pursue anesthetics until achieving a more benign morphology ( ). Quantitative EEG indices based on graph theory analyses can also predict SE recurrence but are currently not readily available at the bedside [ ]. There is no available evidence or experts’ recommendation on how to wean anesthetics. It seems reasonable to progressively taper the infusion rate over several hours to minimize the risk of withdrawal seizures and SE recurrence although the half-life of midazolam and barbiturates could allow for faster taper. In any case, it is critical to closely monitor the EEG during the weaning process, and for at least 24 h afterward, to watch for withdrawal seizures and SE recurrence. If this occurs, the anesthetic should be restarted at the rate that achieved seizure control or another anesthetic might be tried to achieve seizure control. Clinicians should also be aware that non-epileptic rhythmic or periodic patterns, sometimes called generalized periodic discharges related to anesthetic withdrawal (GRAW), might emerge during the weaning process ( ) [ , ]. These patterns generally differ from the ictal features observed prior to anesthesia and should not be confused with SE recurrence: they spontaneously disappear after a few hours, and do not need to be treated with anesthetics. Overall, continuous EEG is helpful at all treatment stages during RSE, allowing diagnosis of ongoing non-convulsive SE after cessation of convulsions, detect breakthrough seizures, and guide the weaning process. It is, thus, not surprising that EEG-guided therapy has been associated with shorter duration of anesthetic exposure [ ]. Complications arising during RSE treatment are mostly caused by prolonged unconsciousness and immobility ( ). A full discussion is beyond the scope of this review and readers are referred to the existing literature [ ]. Side effects can also result from specific compounds, again with barbiturates having a less favorable safety profile than midazolam or propofol, especially in terms of infection risk and hypotension requiring vasopressors. Rarely, prolonged high-dose propofol treatment is associated with the propofol-related infusion syndrome [ ]. Similarly, prolonged exposure to high-dose pentobarbital poses a risk of systemic toxicity of its solvent, propylene glycol [ ]. Of note, this can also arise with the administration in a short amount of time of high doses of other agents associated with propylene glycol, including lorazepam, phenobarbital, or etomidate. Tachyphylaxis is seen commonly with midazolam infusions, requiring higher dose over time and possibly the starting additional ASM. All anesthetics are frequently accompanied by hypotension and respiratory compromise and barbiturates may cause immunosuppression. Additional strategies: super-refractory status epilepticus A permanent response to anesthetics can be expected in up to two-thirds of RSE episodes. Risk factors of SRSE are similar to RSE, with most cases related to acute symptomatic or undetermined etiologies [ , , ]. Many treatment options can be considered, which, however, are supported by even less evidence than RSE treatment of ( ). A first approach consists in reinstating an anesthetic, using the same (if seizures were controlled on previous attempts) or a different compound; combining two agents or more might be necessary to achieve seizure control (i.e., propofol with midazolam). At this stage, hypotension and cardiac depression might become a significant issue limiting further intensification of anesthetic therapy. Ketamine may represent an attractive option, as it has a different mechanism of action, NMDA (glutamate) receptor antagonism, and possesses cardiac and pressure supportive effects. In retrospective studies, it was found to have an efficacy between 30 and 60% and, importantly, to be safe (including lack of increased intracranial pressure) even at doses up to 15 mg/kg.h [ - ]. Its place in the treatment algorithm of RSE and SRSE has not been evaluated in trials, but we suggest using it either in RSE, in association with midazolam or propofol to mitigate their negative circulatory effects, or in the early stage of SRSE, after failure of the first general anesthetic attempt, again combining it with a GABA-ergic agent (details are found in ). While not a first choice for RSE, thiopental and pentobarbital may be used for SRSE, with seizure control in up to 80% [ ]. Complications are almost inevitable and include infections and hypotension; it should be kept in mind that many of these may be associated with the SRSE episode itself, rather than the treatment. There is also renewed interest in phenobarbital, administered as continuous intravenous infusion; high serum levels might be needed, often above the usual range for chronic epilepsy (20–40 μg/dl) [ ]; in our experience, this represents a valuable option for SRSE patients difficult to withdraw from anesthetics. There is limited evidence that inhalational anesthetics, such as isoflurane or desflurane, might help achieving SRSE control; however, they are associated with frequent and severe adverse effects, including hypotension and the practical difficulty to provide a close circuit to prevent leakage to the ICU environment [ ]. Non-sedating ASMs can also be used at the stage of SRSE, often in combination with anesthetics, but only anecdotal evidence is available. It seems logical to favor drugs that can be administered intravenously for quicker action and to circumvent some of the pharmacokinetic changes of critical illness, including lower enteral absorption. In general, high loading and maintenance doses have been used. For any used ASM and anesthetic, interactions and pharmacokinetics changes need to be carefully considered and close monitoring of serum drug levels is advised. Aside from anesthetics and ASMs, non-pharmacological interventions can be tried in SRSE, although evidence is even weaker. Among them, the ketogenic diet, through enteral or IV formulation, seems promising, and has been described in children [ ] and adults [ , ]. While ketosis can be sometimes difficult to achieve, this represents a treatment of choice for SE due to mitochondrial disorders, in which, for example, valproate or propofol is contraindicated. Further non-pharmacological interventions include electroconvulsive therapy [ ], electrical brain stimulation [ ], and neurosurgical resection [ ]. The latter is only feasible for focal SE and should be performed only if a clearly delineated epileptogenic lesion is identified. Hypothermia was studied in a randomized trial and did not show a significant therapeutic impact, pending numerous limitations such as patient selection (i.e., several patients not being in RSE), the chosen treatment protocol, and outcome measures [ ]. Etiology-driven treatment As many as 15% of patients with NORSE or FIRES have antibody-mediated autoimmune encephalitis [ , , ]; seizure control in these cases is rarely achieved with ASM and anesthetics, and immune therapies are almost always required. We recommend starting with high-dose methylprednisolone (1 g/day over 3–5 days) combined with IV immunoglobulins (0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days) or plasma exchange (5–7 exchanges), followed by rituximab, in patients with proven or suspected antibody-mediated encephalitis. As early treatment in these cases is associated with better outcomes, prompt screening for pathogenic antibodies and other unusual causes of SE is important to optimize management [ , ]. Interactions between immune therapies, especially plasma exchanges, and ASM should be carefully assessed. In 50–75% of cases, NORSE and FIRES remain unexplained despite an extensive etiological work-up [ , , ]. These are possibly caused by post-infectious autoinflammatory mechanisms leading to the over-activation of the innate immune system, with high serum and CSF levels of pro-epileptogenic cytokines causing SE [ , ]. Some of these patients appear to respond to compounds acting on the Interleukin (IL)-1β and IL-6 pathways, such as anakinra [ ] and tocilizumab [ ], respectively, and to intrathecal steroid administration [ ]. Treatments with a higher efficacy-to-safety ratio than anesthetics, such as neurosteroids acting as allosteric modulators of GABA receptors, are currently investigated [ ]. Based on animal models, early rational polytherapy, combining an ASM, a benzodiazepine, and an NMDAR antagonist, might potentially decrease the proportion of early SE transitioning to RSE and SRSE [ , ]. Efforts to improve water solubility of ASM that are currently available only as oral formulation, such as topiramate, are underway and will likely extend the armamentarium of drugs that can be used at all stages of SE [ ]. SE in hypoxic–ischemic encephalopathy Up to 1/3 of comatose patients following cardiac arrest may present electrographic (usually with diffuse periodic or rhythmic patterns) and/or clinical (mostly myoclonic) seizure activity [ ]. While this association was regarded as an almost invariable sign of poor prognosis, in the last years converging evidence showed that a small proportion of those with post-anoxic SE may be successfully treated and awaken reaching good cognitive performance. In this context, a multimodal prognostic approach is mandatory, integrating clinical (brainstem reflexes, motor response), neurophysiological (EEG, somatosensory evoked potentials -SSEP), biological (essentially neuron-specific enolase), and radiological investigations [ , ]. This helps determining early if the patient suffers from malignant (myoclonic) SE, heralding a catastrophic prognosis and in whom antiseizure treatment is likely futile, or rather a form of Lance–Adams syndrome, which is much more uncommon but well compatible with awakening upon treatment [ ]. Timing of SE and/or myoclonus (the earlier, under pharmacological sedation, the worse) and of underlying EEG background recovery (the earlier the better) [ , ], electrographic semiology (high-voltage, diffuse and possibly identical poly-spikes on a suppressed background strongly correlate with poor prognosis, unlike lower-voltage spikes centered around the midline and superimposed on a recognizable, ideally reactive background) [ ], return of brainstem reflexes, present cortical SSEP responses [ ], and lack of widespread diffusion-weighted MRI abnormalities [ ] indicate possible recovery upon treatment. A recently proposed EEG-based score (NEC2RAS) may help orienting on the prognosis of these patients [ ]. Although no benefit of treatment of repetitive, periodic or ictal EEG discharges was demonstrated in a randomized controlled trial [ ], the study was underpowered to investigate the effect in these crucially different categories, and multimodal prognostication to stratify patients was not applied. In fact, a post hoc analysis suggested a possible benefit of treatment in seizure patterns. Based on our experience, we recommend the use of ASM with anti-myoclonic properties, such as intravenous benzodiazepines together with valproate and levetiracetam; in treatment refractory patients with otherwise favorable multimodal prognostic assessment consideration of perampanel or zonisamide through the nasogastric tube, as well as escalation to propofol and/or midazolam perfusions for up to 1–2 weeks, may be reasonable [ , ]. Prognosis Surprisingly at first glance, SE mortality did not change significantly over the last 3 decades [ ]. This may be related to the evolving nature of SE types; for instance, more widespread EEG use in the ICU is related to increasing nonconvulsive SE detection over time [ , ]; these patients are more severely ill than those readily diagnosed on the emergency room. Overall SE short-term mortality lies around 10–15% [ , ], and seems to be rather related to the underlying background (increasing age with reduced biological reserve, etiologies directly implying a risk of death, medical comorbidities) [ ], than on specific treatment itself. Use of adequate benzodiazepines doses seem to favor a rapid SE control [ , ], but does not appear to influence its final outcome [ ]. Long-term mortality is also increased after SE, particularly in the first 2 years [ ]. SE refractoriness represents a prognostic marker: mortality increases from 10% in responsive cases, to 25% in RSE and nearly 40% in SRSE [ ]. Existing SE prognostic scores consider increasing age, seizure semiology, lack of previous seizures (as a surrogate of an acute brain insult), and extent of consciousness impairment [ ], or increasing age, etiology, comorbidities, and EEG type [ ], as prognostic factors. Due to the marked variability of clinical presentations and patients’ characteristics, no single predictor has a robust prognostic value. Further, the accuracy of these scores is moderate to fair only, especially in the ICU setting. Other, more subtle prognostic aspects should also be considered. Due to the marked variability of clinical presentations and patients’ characteristics, no single predictor has a robust prognostic value. Further, the accuracy of these scores is moderate to fair only, especially in the ICU setting. Other, more subtle prognostic aspects should also be considered. The risk of developing epilepsy is increased by about three times following SE (particularly RSE) compared to a self-limited seizure [ ]. Assessment of cognitive sequelae following SE is difficult to disentangle from the underlying cause and comorbidities. Compared to epilepsy patients lacking SE episodes, those with SE do not seem to be more impaired on neuropsychological testing, although they are less performant than controls without epilepsy [ ]. Conclusion and outlook SE is a potentially dangerous condition; mortality ranges from 10 to 15% in the short term, and additional long-term effects such as development of epilepsy, cognitive decline, and long-term mortality have been reported. SE needs to be managed urgently, with initial therapy including rapid administration of a benzodiazepine and one among (fos-)phenytoin, levetiracetam, or valproate. Refractory generalized convulsive SE, including subtle post-convulsive SE, is managed with continuous infusions of propofol or midazolam and barbiturates, or other non-pharmacologic treatments; in case of focal SE without major consciousness impairment, general anesthetics may be differed. More important than the choice of treatment is the adherence to existing guidelines. EEG is required for the detection of nonconvulsive seizures and crucial in the management of patients with RSE, as these seizures are almost exclusively nonconvulsive. Addressing the underlying cause of SE is crucial, particularly for patients with treatable conditions such as autoimmune encephalitis. Given the several current knowledge gaps, future studies should focus especially on RSE and SRSE patients, for example testing innovative pharmacological compounds including the timing and type of immunomodulatory interventions, addressing optimal EEG targets and weaning strategies (ideally conducted as randomized trials), and exploring early biomarkers and potential biological targets of pharmacological interventions (as cohort studies).

chunks.content: Lamotrigine (LTG) is an effective prophylactic agent for bipolar disorder and is used to treat a variety of psychiatric disorders. In addition, it is a broad‐spectrum antiepileptic drug, the first‐line therapy for focal seizures in children and adults, and has shown efficacy against generalized seizures. Moreover, LTG is less teratogenic and preferred for girls and women of childbearing potential. Given these characteristics, LTG plays a crucial role in the treatment of psychiatric and neurological diseases. Despite its therapeutic benefits, LTG is associated with severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCARs), such as Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, which can be life‐threatening in rare cases. , Factors associated with SCARs in patients taking LTG include concomitant use of valproic acid (VPA), doses exceeding the protocol, age younger than 13 years, history of rash from other antiepileptic drugs, and being within 8 weeks of LTG treatment. One of these factors, high serum concentrations of LTG in the early stages of administration, is associated with the development of rashes. , , , LTG is primarily metabolized by uridine diphosphate (UDP)‐glucuronosyltransferase (UGT) to LTG N2‐glucuronide. , VPA is a UGT inhibitor, and its concomitant use decreases the total clearance of LTG and increases its elimination half‐life. , , As a result, VPA increases the LTG concentration and risk of rash ; therefore, when used in combination with VPA, the starting LTG dose should be significantly lower than the usual dose. , Previously, a variety of drugs have been reported as UGT inhibitors in vitro. , These include nonsteroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs, benzodiazepines, tricyclic antidepressants, and immunosuppressants. The interaction between LTG and VPA is widely known, whereas no other drugs have been proven to increase the serum concentrations of LTG in humans by inhibiting UGT. Bipolar disorder and epilepsy are often treated using a combination with other medications. , Furthermore, several drugs for other diseases may be used in combination, which may increase the risk of rashes in clinical practice. Therefore, drugs that affect rashes must be identified to ensure safe treatment. Accordingly, we used multiple sets of clinical data to identify concomitant drugs that increase the risk of LTG‐induced rashes. The aim of this study was to determine the impact of other drugs used in combination with LTG on the risk of rash. Methods Risk of rash associated with <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">LTG</styled-content> use in combination with other drugs using <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">VigiBase</styled-content> Data sources VigiBase is a World Health Organization global pharmacovigilance database designed to collect and analyze adverse drug reaction reports worldwide. This study uses the VigiBase data set collected in December 2021. Since VigiBase contains duplicate reports, those considered as duplicates by the Uppsala Monitoring Centre were excluded from the analysis using statistical algorithms. Informed consent was not required because no therapeutic intervention was conducted and an anonymized global open database was used. SCAR was defined using the four terms of Severe Cutaneous Adverse Reactions (SMQ 20000020)” according to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) version 26.0 (Table ). The risk of adverse events was assessed using the reporting odds ratios (RORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Patients administered LTG were classified into four groups: those who (A) used a certain drug and reported SCAR, (B) used a certain drug and did not report SCAR, (C) did not use a certain drug and reported SCAR, and (D) did not use a certain drug and did not report SCAR. Based on the following equations, the RORs and 95% CIs were calculated for each drug. ROR = AD / BC 95 % CI = exp ln ROR ± 1.96 √ 1 / A + 1 / B + 1 / C + 1 / D A significant association between drug use and an increased incidence of SCAR was determined if the lower limit of the 95% CI exceeded 1. Conversely, a significant association between drug use and a decreased incidence of SCAR was determined if the upper limit of the 95% CI was <1. As the present study was retrospective in nature and used existing information, an opt‐out option was displayed on the institution's website as a surrogate for informed consent for eligible patients, according to the Japanese Governmental guidelines. This study was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. As the present study was retrospective in nature and used existing information, an opt‐out option was displayed on the institution's website as a surrogate for informed consent for eligible patients, according to the Japanese Governmental guidelines. Patients were included if they initiated LTG treatment at one of the participating centers between 1 January 2009, and 31 December 2019, and were at least 18 years old. Patients were excluded if they were administered LTG for indications other than bipolar disorder or epilepsy and had never taken LTG after initiation. Data collection and definitions We collected baseline data related to sex, age, initiating dose of LTG, concomitant VPA use, concomitant enzyme inducer (medications that decrease the concentration of LTG; Table ) use, other concomitant medications, and disease history at the initiation of LTG treatment obtained through electronic medical records from Tokushima University Hospital and Asahikawa Medical University Hospital. The presence or absence of rash with LTG was determined from each hospital's medical records, referring to the term “Skin and Subcutaneous Tissue Disorders” in MedDRA version 26.0. Patients were followed up for a period of 24 weeks after the initiation of LTG to allow for sufficient evaluation of rash incidence. Follow‐up was terminated if the patient discontinued LTG during this period. Propensity score matching analysis As patients in this retrospective case‐control study were not randomized to groups treated with or without flunitrazepam (FNZ), propensity score matching (PSM) was performed to decrease variability between cohorts. Six factors (sex, age, disease, LTG starting dose, concomitant VPA use, and concomitant enzyme inducer use) were selected as important demographic characteristics associated with LTG‐induced rash in a logistic regression model used to calculate propensity scores (Table ). A 1:1 PSM analysis was performed using the nearest neighbor matching method with a caliper of 0.20 to reduce the potential bias of patient characteristics. Patients who did not meet the matching criteria were excluded. Prospective observational study of <styled-content style="fixed-case" toggle="no">LTG</styled-content> concentration Population and data collection We performed a prospective observational study in patients who underwent LTG treatment at Tokushima University Hospital, Tokushima, Japan, between 1 May 2023, and 30 April 2024, with the approval of the ethics committee of Tokushima University Hospital (reference number 4228). This study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The participants provided written informed consent before enrollment. Patients were included if they were taking LTG at the same dose for at least 2 weeks and were at least 18 years old. Patients were excluded if they took concomitant medications that affected the LTG concentration (VPA, enzyme inducers). Serum samples for trough values could not be obtained. We collected data related to sex, age, disease history, weight, LTG dose, concomitant medications, and laboratory values using electronic medical records from the Tokushima University Hospital. Laboratory values included aspartate aminotransferase (AST), alanine aminotransferase (ALT), creatinine, and serum urea nitrogen (BUN). Discussion This study utilized multiple sets of clinical data to identify the concomitant medications that increased the risk of LTG‐induced rashes. The results of the VigiBase analysis and retrospective case‐control study showed that concomitant FNZ use increased the incidence of LTG‐induced rashes. In addition, the prospective observational study showed that concomitant FNZ use increased LTG concentration. These results suggest that FNZ may inhibit UGT, leading to increased LTG concentration and a heightened risk of LTG‐induced rash. Notably, previous studies have reported no significant increase in LTG concentrations by drugs other than VPA. However, the present study demonstrates that FNZ significantly elevates the C/D ratio of LTG. Given that FNZ is commonly used as a sleep aid, its potential risk of exacerbating LTG‐induced skin reactions should be carefully considered in clinical practice. LTG is widely used in the fields of psychiatry and neurology. LTG‐induced rashes may develop into fatal SCARs, such as Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis. For LTG to be used safely, the risk of rashes must be minimized. The mechanism of LTG‐induced rashes is not fully understood but has been reported to involve sulfotransferase pathways, LTG itself, drug‐specific T cells, and the human leukocyte antigen. , , , A rapid increase in LTG concentration during the early stages of administration is associated with the development of rashes. , , , Since concomitant VPA use increases LTG concentration, the LTG dose is controlled to prevent the onset of rash. The treatment of bipolar disorder and epilepsy is often combined with other medications, which may affect the risk of rash. In the medical big data analysis using VigiBase, concomitant FNZ and VPA use was shown to significantly increase the ROR of SCAR. Among other benzodiazepines, concomitant nitrazepam use also increased the ROR of SCAR, whereas diazepam, clonazepam, and lorazepam did not. The incidence of LTG‐induced rash was similar to that reported in previous studies and was considered adequately evaluated. When LTG was combined with FNZ, the incidence of rashes significantly increased in the PSM analysis, suggesting an additional effect of FNZ on rash risk. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first prospective observational study to report that medications other than VPA increase LTG concentration in humans. LTG exhibits first‐order linear pharmacokinetics, with its concentration increasing in a dose‐dependent manner. Drug interactions have been reported to alter C/D ratio, with the C/D ratio increasing approximately 2.2‐fold when LTG and VPA were combined. The C/D ratio of the LTG without FNZ group in our study and of the LTG monotherapy group in a controlled clinical trial in Japanese patients showed similar results. In our study, we found that FNZ significantly increased the LTG C/D ratio. We also examined the effects of LTG on its metabolites. The N2‐glucuronide/LTG ratio reflects LTG glucuronide conjugation and decreases as the metabolism slows down. This ratio is useful for identifying the metabolic effects of concomitant medications and pregnancy. , The N2‐glucuronide/LTG ratio of 0.54 in the LTG group found by Yang et al . was similar to the respective value of the LTG without FNZ group in our study (0.51). The N2‐glucuronide/LTG ratio was lower in the LTG with FNZ group than in the LTG without FNZ group. These results suggest that FNZ inhibits LTG metabolism. LTG is primarily metabolized by UGT1A4 and various UGT isoforms, such as UGT1A3, UGT2B7, and UGT2B10, are also involved in its metabolism. , , The mechanism by which VPA increases LTG concentration has been reported to involve the inhibition of UGT2B7 and 2B10. , Some reports have indicated that FNZ inhibits UGT. For example, it was shown that FNZ exhibits potent competitive inhibition of rat liver morphine UGT activity. Another study showed that FNZ inhibited glucuronidation of 3′‐azido‐3′‐deoxythymidine in the human liver. In addition, FNZ inhibited UGT2B7 as well as VPA in vitro. In our prospective observational study, FNZ increased the LTG concentration, likely in association with UGT inhibition. Our study has some limitations. In the VigiBase analysis, the ROR of SCAR was significantly increased when nitrazepam was combined with LTG. We attempted to investigate the risk of rash with concomitant nitrazepam use, but both retrospective and prospective studies were unable to evaluate the small number of patients receiving nitrazepam concomitantly. The effects of benzodiazepines other than FNZ also need to be tested in large cohort studies. A retrospective cohort study reported that rashes during LTG administration were not always related to drug hypersensitivity. Other rashes unlikely to be caused by LTG were more common in children than adults. Our retrospective case‐control study did not include children, and the occurrence of other rashes unlikely to be caused by LTG is considered low. In this prospective study, we evaluated factors affecting LTG concentration but were unable to examine UGT gene polymorphisms. UGT1A4 and UGT2B7 genetic polymorphisms may affect LTG concentration. , Moreover, different frequencies of the UGT mutant alleles have been reported among different ethnic groups. Furthermore, a higher risk of SCAR owing to LTG has been reported in Asian patients. Another limitation of our study is that it only included Japanese patients. Validation in a larger multiethnic sample is needed. In addition, since the LTG maintenance dose was evaluated at the trough LTG steady‐state concentration, it was not possible to prospectively examine the effect of LTG concentration during the early administration period on the risk of rash. Further detailed prospective studies are required. Conclusions This study showed that FNZ increased LTG serum concentration and increased the risk of rash.
